claims.text: Rapid quenching immediately after low-temperature synthesis kinetically freezes the multi-element solid-solution state.
A quenched atomic configuration retains limited atomic mobility during subsequent high-temperature service.
Limited atomic mobility prevents diffusion-driven phase segregation.
Limited atomic mobility prevents diffusion-driven coarsening.
Near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles can be formed from a single-source precursor at low temperature.
Rapid cooling produces a kinetically trapped, highly disordered atomic arrangement.
Inhibiting atomic or precursor mobility favors formation of a single-phase high-entropy nanoparticle.
Mobility inhibition imposed during post-synthesis quenching persists sufficiently to suppress diffusion during later high-temperature operation.
Rapid quenching suppresses sintering during subsequent high-temperature service.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will remain structurally and chemically uniform during service at 773–1173 K.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will remain stable over the thermoelectric service range of 473–1923 K.
Relative to slow cooling, rapid quenching will yield less grain growth, phase separation, agglomeration, and compositional inhomogeneity under identical service conditions.
Slow cooling increases atomic mobility during cooling and thereby promotes elemental segregation or coarsening.
The proposed quench-stabilization mechanism may not apply to nanoparticles synthesized by high-temperature shock or other high-mobility methods.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to compositions that deviate substantially from near-equiatomic ratios.
Failure of the quenched batch to show significantly less segregation, sintering, or compositional inhomogeneity than the slow-cooled control would falsify the hypothesis.
